title: Count on an abacus: beads that hold a number
description: Long before calculators, shopkeepers across Asia counted with beads on rods — and the abacus is still faster than fingers. Learn how one rod holds ones, the next tens, and how a number lives in the beads.

body.heading: Meet the rods
paragraphs: A school abacus has rows or rods of beads, and each rod stands for a place in a number: ones, tens, hundreds. On a Japanese-style soroban each rod has one bead above the bar and four below it; on a classroom counting frame, ten beads slide on each wire. Either way, the rule is the same — a bead only counts when it is pushed to its counting position.
Start with everything cleared: no beads touching the bar. That empty, quiet frame is zero, and every number you will ever make is just beads moved with intent.

body.heading: Build numbers, then add
paragraphs: Slide beads to show 7 on the ones rod. Now add 5 more: there are not enough ones beads left, so trade — clear the ones and push one bead on the tens rod, then show the remaining 2. You have just done carrying with your hands, the move written maths hides inside a tiny 1.
Race a partner: one of you calls a number up to 99, the other builds it. Then swap. Finish with shopkeeper sums — build the price, build the payment, slide back the change.

takeaway: Each rod is a place — ones, tens, hundreds — and 'carrying' stops being a rule in a book and becomes a trade your hands can feel.
materials: A school counting-frame abacus or soroban-style abacus
A partner for the number race (optional)
Paper and pencil to write the numbers you build
supervision: No special supervision is needed; an adult or older child can act as the number-caller for younger players.
safetyNotes: Check a second-hand abacus for loose beads or splintered rods before play, and keep loose beads away from toddlers, who may put them in their mouths.
Play on a table so a dropped abacus cannot land on feet.
